steps.say: A diaphragm that sits too high and barely moves may be weak from birth, stunned by a birth injury, or cut during heart surgery. The phrenic nerve usually carries the blame.
steps.tx: A high still hemidiaphragm has three usual causes. **Eventration** (floppy high diaphragm) means an abnormally high half diaphragm from congenital weakness, from birth trauma with upper plexus **Erb palsy** (shoulder birth injury) of **C5 to C6** (fifth to sixth neck nerves) that can include the **C3 to C5** (third to fifth neck nerves) **phrenic nerve** (breathing nerve) in extensive injuries, or from acquired phrenic injury during cardiac surgery. Each cause weakens the sheet, so it rides up into the chest.

steps.say: Watch the diaphragm move on screening to confirm the diagnosis. A sheet that sits still or climbs when it should fall marks eventration, and that split-second motion separates it from a true hernia.
steps.tx: Motion testing separates a weak sheet from a hole. **Fluoroscopy** (live X ray movie) or ultrasound showing absent or **paradoxical movement** (wrong way motion) on inspiration confirms eventration and separates it from **diaphragmatic hernia** (true hole) on plain radiograph. In a hernia, bowel shadows fill the chest, while in eventration the liver or spleen humps up under an intact but floppy sheet.

steps.say: A floppy diaphragm that still breathes adequately can be left alone. When the baby labours or cannot leave the ventilator, surgeons fold and stitch the sheet tight.
steps.tx: Symptoms decide, not the height alone. Repair is indicated for distress or **ventilator dependence** (stuck on breathing machine), done open or laparoscopically by **diaphragm plication** (folding the sheet tight) with multiple interrupted **nonabsorbable sutures** (permanent stitches). Plication flattens the dome so the lung below can expand, and most babies wean from support soon after.

steps.say: One lobe can overinflate like a balloon that never empties, mostly in baby boys in the first months. Weak airway cartilage lets air in but not out.
steps.tx: An overinflated lobe in a young infant has a classic cause. **Congenital lobar emphysema** (balloon lobe disease) affects **1 in 20000 to 30000 births** (one in twenty thousand to thirty thousand births) with a **3 to 1** (three to one) male excess in the first **6 months** (six months), from deficient **bronchial cartilage** (floppy airway rings) causing expiratory collapse and **air trapping** (stuck air). Air enters easily and leaves poorly, so the lobe swells.

steps.say: Know which lobe balloons most often, and never mistake that bright lucency for a collapsed lung needing a chest tube. A drain stabbed into trapped lobe air is a disaster.
steps.tx: Lobe address and one deadly mimic complete the picture. The **left upper lobe** (top left lobe) leads at **43 percent** (forty three percent), then the right middle lobe at **32 percent** (thirty two percent) and the right upper lobe at **21 percent** (twenty one percent). On **chest radiograph** (chest X ray film) the lucency must never be mistaken for a **pneumothorax** (collapsed lung), since a chest drain into emphysematous lobe air injures without helping.

steps.say: Forced breaths from the ventilator worsen the trapping, so handle these babies gently. When the chest centre keeps shifting and the baby keeps failing, remove the lobe promptly through an open cut.
steps.tx: Ventilation strategy can harm before surgery saves. Positive pressure ventilation worsens **auto-PEEP** (self made end pressure) in these infants, stacking breath upon breath in the trapped lobe. Progressive **mediastinal shift** (pushed chest centre) with worsening symptoms needs prompt open **lobectomy** (lobe removal), since the swelling lobe crushes the good lung and twists its vessels.

steps.say: A leftover bud from the early windpipe can sit silently near the airway for years. Scans show a smooth fluid ball that never lights up with contrast, sitting by the carina when it formed early.
steps.tx: A foregut bud left behind becomes a quiet cyst. **Bronchogenic cysts** (windpipe bud cysts) arise at **3 to 6 weeks** (three to six weeks) of gestation in **1 in 42000 to 68000 births** (one in forty two thousand to sixty eight thousand births) with male excess. They sit near the **carina** (windpipe fork) and right hilum when early and peripheral when late, and appear as nonenhancing mucus filled spheres on **computed tomography** (contrast CT scan).

vis.alt: Microscopic view of a bronchogenic cyst wall with ciliated respiratory lining over smooth muscle.
vis.caption: Microscopic cyst wall with respiratory lining. On CT these cysts are nonenhancing mucus filled spheres near the carina. Credit: Monika Kujdowicz, CC BY-SA 4.0.

steps.say: Every such cyst comes out, even one found by chance, because pressure, infection and rare cancer change all threaten. Lung buried cysts usually join a bronchus while chest centre ones usually end blind.
steps.tx: Silence is no excuse to leave one in place. All bronchogenic cysts need **surgical resection** (planned removal) even when silent, because **airway compression** (squeezed windpipe), infection and rare **malignant transformation** (cancer change) threaten. Parenchymal cysts usually communicate with a bronchus and mediastinal ones usually end blind, but both share the same fate on the operating list.

vis.caption: Middle compartment, a favourite seat of bronchogenic cysts. Every cyst is resected even when silent. Credit: StewardMD.
